widget.solution:
import math
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

def direction_report(returns, n_train):
    # features without look-ahead, time split, scaler + logistic regression in a Pipeline
    # return (hit_rate, base_rate, t_vs_base, auc), each rounded to 4 places
    X, y = [], []
    for t in range(19, len(returns) - 1):
        window = returns[t - 19:t + 1]
        m = sum(window) / 20
        vol = (sum((v - m) ** 2 for v in window) / 20) ** 0.5
        X.append([returns[t], sum(returns[t - 4:t + 1]), vol])
        y.append(1 if returns[t + 1] > 0 else 0)
    model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(C=1.0))
    model.fit(X[:n_train], y[:n_train])
    y_test = y[n_train:]
    pred = model.predict(X[n_train:])
    prob = model.predict_proba(X[n_train:])[:, 1]
    n = len(y_test)
    hit = sum(int(a == b) for a, b in zip(pred, y_test)) / n
    base = sum(y_test) / n
    t = (hit - base) / math.sqrt(base * (1 - base) / n)
    auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, prob)
    return (round(hit, 4), round(base, 4), round(t, 4), round(float(auc), 4))
widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def simulate(n, seed, mu=0.0004, phi=-0.05, gam=-0.03, sigma=0.01):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    e = rng.normal(0, sigma, n)
    r = np.zeros(n)
    for t in range(n):
        prev = r[t - 1] if t >= 1 else 0.0
        week = r[max(0, t - 5):t].sum()
        r[t] = mu + phi * prev + gam * week + e[t]
    return [round(float(v), 6) for v in r]

returns = simulate(1000, 27)
returns_b = simulate(1000, 6)

items.prose: Derive logistic regression's formula for $p$ from the assumption that the log-odds are linear in the features.
items.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $p = \dfrac{e^{z}}{1 + e^{z}} = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$: divide, then divide top and bottom by $e^{z}$

feedback.correct: Exponentiate, clear the fraction, collect, divide: the sigmoid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Undo the log first, then solve for $p$.

byKey.c: Clearing the fraction needs the odds written without a log first.
byKey.d: Collecting $p$ terms needs the fraction cleared first.

explain.text: Each step keeps the equation true. The last form keeps $p$ inside $(0, 1)$ for every $z$. The straight line of lesson 10 could not.

items.prose: A colleague asks how to evaluate a new default classifier on 5 years of loans.
items.question: Put the steps of an honest evaluation in order.

lines.text: Split by time: the oldest 4 years to train, the latest year to test, untouched
Fit the scaler and the model on the training years only
Choose the threshold from the costs, on training-year predictions
Score the test year once: precision, recall, AUC and a reliability diagram
Compare with the base rate and “always no”, with standard errors

feedback.correct: Every fitted choice happens before the test year is opened, and the result is judged against a baseline.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Nothing may be fitted or chosen after the test year is looked at.

byKey.fit: The split must come first, or the scaler sees the test year.
byKey.tune: The threshold is chosen after the model is fitted, and before testing.
byKey.score: Scoring comes after every choice is fixed.
byKey.base: The comparison needs the test scores.

explain.text: Split, fit, choose, score once, compare. Any loop back from the test year to an earlier step turns it into training data.

items.title: The 72% crash predictor
items.prompt: A colleague announces a “72% accurate crash predictor”. It calls each trading day “crash” or “no crash”, where a crash is a fall of more than 3%. In the data, 3% of days are crashes. Write a note to your desk head covering three points. (a) What 72% accuracy means here, and how it compares with a trivial rule. (b) The five things you would ask for. (c) What result would convince you the predictor is worth using.
items.model:
**(a) What 72% means.** Accuracy counts right calls on all days. With crashes on 3% of days, the rule “never crash” is right 97% of the time. So 72% is 25 points *worse* than doing nothing. A predictor scores 72% only by calling crash on many calm days. If it caught every crash, its false alarms would be about $1 - 0.72 = 28\%$ of days. Then at best roughly 3 of every 31 crash calls would be real, a precision near 0.10.

**(b) What to ask for.**
1. The confusion matrix on a held-out period: true and false positives and negatives, not accuracy.
2. Precision and recall for crashes, and the ROC and precision-recall curves with AUC, so the threshold is not hiding anything.
3. How the test was built: a time-ordered split, features computed without look-ahead, the threshold chosen on training data. There should be no shuffled cross-validation of overlapping windows.
4. How many crashes the test period contains. With 3% of 1,000 days, about 30, so any recall has a standard error near $\sqrt{0.5 \times 0.5/30} = 0.09$.
5. Calibration, if the output is a probability that will size hedges: a reliability diagram on held-out days.

**(c) What would convince me.** On a test period the model never touched, I want three things. Precision should be well above the 3% base rate (say 0.15 or more) with useful recall. The precision-recall curve should sit clearly above the base-rate line. The test should hold enough crashes that the gain is several standard errors. Then the economic test: after each hedge's cost, does hedging on its calls beat never hedging and always hedging? Only that last number decides whether anyone uses it.

rubric.text: Compares 72% with the 97% of “never crash” and explains that accuracy is dominated by the base rate
Infers that the model must raise many false alarms, so precision is low
Asks for the confusion matrix, precision and recall (or ROC/PR curves and AUC) instead of accuracy
Asks about leakage: time-ordered split, no look-ahead, threshold chosen on training data
Notes the small number of crashes in a test period and the resulting uncertainty
States a convincing result: precision well above the base rate on untouched data, by several standard errors. Adds a P&L test after hedging costs

items.prose: A lender refuses loans above a threshold. A wrongly refused loan loses £3,000 of margin; a missed default loses £30,000. The model is calibrated.
items.question: What threshold minimises the expected cost? Give 3 decimal places.

byKey.ratio: $3{,}000/30{,}000$ leaves the false-alarm cost out of the denominator.
byKey.swap: You put the miss cost on top.

explain.text: Refuse when $(1 - p) \times 3{,}000 < p \times 30{,}000$, so $p > 1/11 = 0.091$. If the probabilities were overconfident, this threshold would refuse the wrong loans.

items.prose: A default model has coefficient 0.40 on leverage. A loan has default probability 0.10. Its leverage rises by 3 turns, the rest fixed.
items.question: What is its new default probability? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Three turns add $3 \times 0.40 = 1.2$ to the log-odds.

byKey.add: You added the change to the probability.
byKey.once: You applied one turn only. Three turns multiply the odds by $e^{1.2}$.
byKey.ratio-p: You multiplied the probability, not the odds, by $e^{1.2}$.

explain.text: The odds $1/9$ become $e^{1.2}/9 = 0.369$, so $p = 0.269$. The odds more than triple; the probability does not quite.

items.prose: A model's true hit rate is 0.53 in a market whose base rate of up days is 0.51.
items.question: How many test days does its edge need to reach two standard errors of the base rate?

byKey.one: That reaches one standard error. Two need four times the days.
byKey.coin: You measured the edge against 0.5. The baseline is 0.51, so the edge is 0.02.

explain.text: $n = 4b(1-b)/\delta^2 = 2,499$ trading days, about ten years, and the edge must survive costs as well.

items.prose: Even-money bets truly win with probability 0.58, so Kelly stakes $2p - 1 = 0.16$. An overconfident model says 0.70 and stakes 0.40.
items.question: What is the long-run growth per bet at a stake of 0.40? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the true 0.58 with a stake of 0.40.

byKey.kelly: 0.0129 is the growth at the Kelly stake 0.16.
byKey.model: You used the model's 0.70. The bets win 58% of the time.

explain.text: At the calibrated stake capital grows 1.29% per bet; at 0.40 it shrinks 1.94%. The edge is real and the overconfidence destroys it.
